cards.front: ADHD prevalence is approximately [___]% in school-age children; highly heritable — family history is the biggest single risk factor.
cards.context:
ADHD affects ~5% of school-age children, M:F ~3:1 (girls more often inattentive presentation, diagnosed later). Highly heritable — family history is the biggest single risk factor.

Typically detected after school entry because school demands sustained attention and quiet behaviour that may be tolerated at home.

Comorbidities common: learning disorders, anxiety, ODD, conduct disorder, autism.

cards.front: Hilar enlargement in cystic fibrosis is due either to adenopathy from chronic infection or to prominent pulmonary arteries from pulmonary [___].
cards.context:
Two things enlarge the hila in cystic fibrosis and they mean different things.

Adenopathy reflects chronic infection. Prominent pulmonary arteries reflect pulmonary hypertension secondary to the lung disease — a later and more ominous finding.

cards.front: Neutropenia is defined on the absolute neutrophil count rather than the [___], so a reassuring total white-cell count can conceal it entirely.
cards.context:
Neutropenia is defined on the ABSOLUTE count, not the share of the differential. A child can have a reassuring total white count of 6 with only 8% neutrophils and be profoundly neutropenic.

The arithmetic is worth doing by hand once: total white cells multiplied by the neutrophil fraction. Laboratories usually report it directly, but the number quoted on a ward round is often the total.

This is why 'the white count is normal' is never an answer to 'is this child neutropenic'.

cards.front: The thriving infant with effortless regurgitation needs parental [___], not acid suppression or investigations.
cards.context:
The natural history is resolution by around a year, so the consult is about explaining that arc to the family — no medication changes it.

Escalate only for GORD features: conservative feeding measures first, then a time-limited acid-suppression trial for marked distress or suspected oesophagitis. Red flags demand investigation, not a PPI.

cards.front: A healthy toddler's plasma creatinine sits at only about [___] µmol/L, far below the adult range, because there is so little muscle to generate it.
cards.context:
The number itself is startling once you see it beside the adult range: a healthy toddler sits around a third of the adult upper limit.

That is the whole reason a comfortable adult creatinine can conceal serious renal impairment in a small child — the value has to double or triple before it looks abnormal to an eye trained on adults.

Because the range is so compressed, small absolute rises matter: a change from 25 to 50 is a halving of function, even though both numbers look trivially small.

cards.front: Most common cause of bronchiolitis is [___]; peak age 3-6 months.
cards.context:
RSV bronchiolitis is the leading cause of paediatric hospitalisation in winter months. Higher risk for severe disease: ex-preterm, congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease, immunocompromised, age <3 months.

Nirsevimab (RSV monoclonal antibody) is now available for high-risk infants and reduces severe RSV disease.

cards.front: A febrile infant aged [___] days or younger by corrected age needs blood, urine and CSF investigation plus admission for empiric intravenous antibiotics.
cards.context:
RCH uses corrected age. An infant aged 28 days or younger with fever needs FBE, CRP, blood culture, an uncontaminated urine specimen, CSF studies and chest imaging when respiratory infection is suspected.

The infant is admitted for empiric IV therapy even if feeding and examination initially look normal.

cards.front: Before adding potassium to a child’s intravenous maintenance fluid, assess electrolytes and [___] function.
cards.context: Impaired excretion can make potassium supplementation hazardous. Use a premixed bag when supplementation is appropriate.

cards.front: Bilirubin that has been processed by the liver and is water-soluble is the [___] fraction.
cards.context:
Conjugation happens IN the liver, attaching glucuronic acid so bilirubin becomes water-soluble and can be excreted in bile and urine. Unconjugated bilirubin is the pre-liver, fat-soluble form bound to albumin.

The split tells you WHERE the problem sits: a rise in the pre-liver fraction points before/at the liver's uptake; a rise in the processed fraction points to the liver or the drainage system below it.

cards.front: Cystic fibrosis (CF) management pillars: [___] clearance, dornase alfa, nebulised hypertonic saline, antibiotics, and pancreatic enzyme replacement.
cards.context:
The five pillars of CF maintenance work together: daily airway clearance — positive expiratory pressure (PEP), active cycle of breathing (ACBT), exercise — prevents mucus stagnation.

Dornase alfa cleaves neutrophil DNA. Antibiotics: empirical for exacerbations, chronic suppressive (inhaled tobramycin for Pseudomonas); pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) for nutrition.

cards.front: Gastro-oesophageal reflux (GOR) is physiological in infants — peaks at 4 months and resolves by [___] months as the lower oesophageal sphincter (LES) matures. Distinguish from GORD (= GOR with complications).
cards.context:
Physiological GOR (gastro-oesophageal reflux) is the 'happy spitter' — frequent regurgitation but normal weight gain, no distress, no respiratory issues. Common in infants because the LES tone is immature.

Peaks ~4 months, resolves by 12-18 months as the LES matures. Pathological GORD = reflux causing complications (FTT, oesophagitis, aspiration).

cards.front: Scarlet fever (Group A Strep, toxin-mediated rash) needs [___] for 10 days; this prevents rheumatic fever but NOT post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
cards.context:
Scarlet fever is the toxin-mediated rash variant of GAS pharyngitis — pyrogenic exotoxins drive the sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, and Pastia's lines.

Antibiotics prevent acute rheumatic fever (cross-reactive autoimmunity vs heart, joints, brain, at 2-4 weeks) but do NOT reliably prevent PSGN.

PSGN is immune-complex nephritis (haematuria + hypertension, at 1-2 weeks); treating the index infection neither averts it nor treats it once established. Complete the full 10-day course to eradicate the organism.

cards.front: The triad of heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, and oedema is [___].
cards.context: Think 'leaky glomerulus': massive protein loss in urine drops serum albumin, and oncotic pressure falls, so fluid moves to tissues (periorbital/peripheral oedema).

cards.front: In an otherwise well child ≥3 months, uncomplicated afebrile cystitis is usually treated orally for about [___] days.
cards.context:
For otherwise well children aged ≥3 months with uncomplicated afebrile cystitis, RCH uses 3–5-day oral courses; eTG uses 3 days for cefalexin or trimethoprim and 5 days for nitrofurantoin.

 Younger or seriously unwell children need an age- and severity-specific pathway. Follow local AMS rather than treating 3 versus 5 days as a hard conflict.

cards.front: Uncontrolled asthma = any [___] features (daytime symptoms, night waking, reliever use, activity limitation); partly controlled = 1-2 features.
cards.context:
The control framework guides stepping up therapy — escalate on the four-feature clinical assessment plus exacerbation frequency, not on FEV1 alone.

Australian thresholds: RCH defines good control as daytime and reliever use under twice weekly, night waking under twice monthly, and no activity limitation.

Some international charts count ANY night waking as loss of control; RCH and AAH both allow up to twice monthly, so use the Australian numbers here.

reference.title: Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)

cards.front: A 13-year-old girl has a painless right thoracic curve, a rib hump on bending forward and a normal neurological examination. The most likely diagnosis is [___].
cards.context:
It is the commonest type and a diagnosis of exclusion: typically a girl around the growth spurt, painless, with normal neurology.

Constant back pain, a left thoracic curve or abnormal neurology breaks the pattern, and the orthopaedic team then orders MRI to look for a syrinx or cord tumour.

cards.front: FPIES: profuse [___] 2-4 hours after ingestion; common triggers include rice, cow's milk, soy.
cards.context:
FPIES is a non-IgE delayed-onset reaction — profuse vomiting 2-4 h after ingestion of trigger food, often with pallor, lethargy, sometimes shock; NO urticaria or other typical allergy features.

Common triggers: rice (paradoxically), cow's milk, soy, oats; skin testing negative; diagnosis clinical. Treatment of acute episode: ondansetron + IV fluids; usually outgrown by 2-4 years.

cards.front: Blood in stool may not be visible — perform [___]; presence of RBCs and leukocytes supports inflammatory colitis.
cards.context:
Faecal occult blood may not be visible to the parent or even on gross inspection — bloody diarrhoea can present as just watery diarrhoea with subtle red discolouration or none at all.

Send stool for routine microscopy + culture in any prolonged or atypical paediatric diarrhoea.

cards.front: Most common bacterial cause of paediatric tonsillitis is Group A [___], peak 5-15 years, rare under 3; treat with phenoxymethylpenicillin to prevent rheumatic fever.
cards.context:
GABHS (S. pyogenes) is the dominant bacterial cause of paediatric tonsillitis — peak 5-15y, rare <3y (immature lymphoid tissue, different flora). Most sore throats in young children are viral.

GABHS needs phenoxymethylpenicillin 10 days, mainly to prevent acute rheumatic fever (antibiotics do NOT prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis).

Tonsillectomy for recurrent cases meeting Paradise criteria (7+/yr, 5/yr for 2y, 3/yr for 3y).

cards.front: Hand-foot-mouth disease (Coxsackie A16) may be followed by nail shedding (onychomadesis) weeks after; this is [___] and needs no treatment.
cards.context:
Onychomadesis (proximal nail-bed separation) follows hand-foot-mouth disease in some children weeks after the acute infection has resolved. The mechanism is temporary nail matrix arrest from systemic viral illness.

Parents often present anxiously after noticing the nails 'falling off' — reassure: self-limiting, nails regrow normally, no treatment needed.

cards.front: In young children pleural effusions are hard to distinguish from other hazy shadowing because most films are taken supine, so fluid layers [___].
cards.context:
Why effusions are harder to call in small children, and it is about positioning rather than the fluid.

Most paediatric films are taken supine, so fluid layers posteriorly instead of collecting at the base. The result is a hazy hemithorax that is difficult to separate from consolidation.

cards.front: A teenager with lupus has inflammation of the pleura and pericardium. The collective term for inflammation of these serous linings is [___].
cards.context: Pleural involvement may cause pain on deep inspiration. Pericardial involvement may cause chest pain that improves on sitting up, linking the shared term to two different clinical patterns.

cards.front: Persistent deficits in social communication plus restricted, repetitive behaviours from early childhood define [___] spectrum disorder.
cards.context: Two core domains, present from early childhood: persistent social-communication deficits AND restricted, repetitive behaviours/interests. Severity and language vary widely (a spectrum).

cards.front: Atopic dermatitis affects [___]% of children, with 85% of childhood cases beginning before age 5. It can precede food allergy, allergic rhinitis and asthma, but this is an increased-risk association rather than a fixed progression.
cards.context:
Eczema affects 10-20% of children; about 85% of childhood cases begin before age 5. It reflects skin-barrier dysfunction and a Th2-skewed immune response.

Early or severe eczema is associated with later food allergy, asthma and allergic rhinitis. The 'atopic march' is a population association, not a fixed sequence; most children do not develop every condition.

cards.front: In a febrile child a [___] appearance (lethargy, poor perfusion, weak cry) is a stronger predictor of serious bacterial infection than the absolute height of the temperature.
cards.context:
In the febrile child the overall appearance — a 'toxic' look of lethargy, poor eye contact, weak cry, mottling and poor perfusion — predicts serious bacterial infection better than the height of the temperature.

A child with a high fever who is playful and consolable is far more reassuring than a quiet, floppy child with a modest fever.

cards.front: Most common cause of bronchiolitis is RSV; peak age [___] months.
cards.context:
RSV bronchiolitis is the leading cause of paediatric hospitalisation in winter months. Higher risk for severe disease: ex-preterm, congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease, immunocompromised, age <3 months.

Nirsevimab (RSV monoclonal antibody) is now available for high-risk infants and reduces severe RSV disease.

cards.front: Phototherapy works by converting unconjugated bilirubin in the skin into a water-soluble structural isomer, [___], which is excreted directly in bile and urine without hepatic conjugation.
cards.context: Lumirubin is the irreversible structural isomer (versus the reversible configurational photoisomers). Because it bypasses hepatic conjugation, phototherapy only lowers UNconjugated bilirubin.

cards.front: An infant has intensely itchy papules and burrows involving the palms and soles; several household members also itch. The most likely infestation is [___].
cards.context: Infant scabies can involve the palms, soles and scalp. Household symptoms help distinguish it from non-contagious eczema.

cards.front: Infantile haemangioma: most common benign soft tissue tumour; 3 phases — proliferative (3-6 months), plateau, involution (50% by age 5); first-line treatment is [___].
cards.context:
Infantile haemangiomas are the commonest benign soft tissue tumour of childhood — not usually present at birth, appear in first weeks.

Most need no treatment.

Treat (oral propranolol first-line) for: ulceration, periorbital (amblyopia risk), nasal tip (anatomic distortion), large, multiple, or symptomatic.

cards.front: An adolescent with exudative tonsillitis develops a maculopapular rash after amoxicillin. The likely underlying infection is EBV; this rash alone neither proves nor excludes penicillin [___].
cards.context:
A maculopapular rash after amoxicillin during EBV infection can be transient, but true drug hypersensitivity also occurs. EBV alone cannot settle the allergy question.

Document the drug, timing and reaction features. Record suspected allergy pending assessment and follow the local drug-allergy pathway; testing belongs in a controlled clinical setting.

cards.front: Cyanosis in TOF depends on RV outflow obstruction: severe TOF may be cyanotic from [___], while milder “pink” TOF may become cyanotic over ensuing months.
cards.context:
Septal defects vastly outnumber every cyanotic lesion, which is why a hole in the ventricular septum tops the overall list.

Among cyanotic lesions the superlatives split by timing: TOF is the biggest group, but severe obstruction may cause cyanosis at birth while milder “pink” TOF declares itself over ensuing months.

TGA cannot wait — its parallel circulations need ductal mixing, so it collapses within days of birth as the duct closes.

cards.front: A child with recurrent chest infections, steatorrhoea, and a high sweat chloride should have the [___] gene assessed.
cards.context: Recurrent sinopulmonary infection plus pancreatic insufficiency and a raised sweat chloride point to cystic fibrosis. CFTR encodes an epithelial chloride channel.

cards.front: Otitis externa affects the ear [___]; cardinal clinical sign is pain when pulling the pinna or pressing the tragus — distinguishes it from otitis media, which affects the middle ear.
cards.context:
Otitis externa is a skin/soft-tissue infection of the external auditory canal — distinct from otitis media (middle ear behind intact TM).

Cardinal sign: pain on pulling pinna or pressing tragus (moves inflamed canal skin) — AOM doesn't cause this.

Topical antibiotic + steroid drops (Sofradex, Ciproxin HC); DON'T syringe (risks pushing infection deeper).

cards.front: Most common bacterial pneumonia organism in children is [___]; Mycoplasma causes 'walking pneumonia' in older children.
cards.context:
The organism shifts with age: Strep pneumoniae dominates classic lobar pneumonia (acute fever, focal consolidation), so amoxicillin is empirical first-line.

Mycoplasma becomes important in school-age children — its 'walking pneumonia' is more gradual with dry cough and patchy changes, and being atypical (no cell wall) it needs a macrolide, not amoxicillin.

cards.front: Neonatal septic shock is often a [___] shock phenotype; give carefully titrated fluid with frequent reassessment and start inotropes early if perfusion remains poor.
cards.context:
Cold shock—with cool mottled skin, prolonged capillary refill and narrow pulse pressure—is common in neonates and infants.

Manage airway and oxygenation, obtain rapid IV or IO access, give early antibiotics and carefully titrated fluid, and reassess after each intervention.

Escalate early to inotropes and critical care when perfusion remains poor rather than waiting for hypotension.

cards.front: In parvovirus B19, infection during roughly the first half of pregnancy risks fetal anaemia and [___].
cards.context:
Because a well child with slapped cheek needs nothing, the useful action is the exposure question rather than a treatment.

A pregnant contact, especially in the first half of pregnancy, should be discussed and may need serology and fetal surveillance for hydrops.

A contact with a haemolytic anaemia needs to know to present early if they become pale, breathless or lethargic. Neither of these is found by examining the child. They are found by asking.

cards.front: The key CXR sign of an inhaled foreign body is [___] on an expiratory film due to the ball-valve effect.
cards.context:
An inhaled foreign body may not be radio-opaque (most are food/plastic).

If clinical suspicion is high but CXR is normal, bronchoscopy is indicated.

cards.front: Fixed target lesions on a child’s hands each have a dark centre, a pale middle ring and a red outer rim. This morphology suggests [___].
cards.context: The three-zone target helps distinguish this eruption from transient urticarial wheals. Check for mucosal involvement and recent herpes simplex symptoms.

cards.front: Pubertal gynaecomastia affects ~80% of normal males in Tanner stages 3-4; usually resolves spontaneously within [___] years.
cards.context:
Pubertal gynaecomastia affects up to 80% of normal males in Tanner stage 3-4 — transient relative oestrogen excess as testosterone production rises.

Refer if persistent (>2 years), severe, or features of underlying pathology (Klinefelter, drug use, sex steroid tumour).

cards.front: With an intact eardrum and normal canal volume, both glue ear and acute otitis media can produce a type B tympanogram; signs of acute [___] separate them.
cards.context:
With an intact eardrum and normal canal volume, a flat trace supports effusion but cannot distinguish glue ear from acute otitis media.

Acute onset and inflammatory otoscopic findings support acute otitis media; glue ear lacks acute inflammation.

cards.front: Typical puberty duration is [___] years; delayed and precocious puberty are defined by gonadarche (FSH/LH-driven gonadal activation), not adrenarche.
cards.context:
Puberty typically lasts 2-5 years from start to completion. The defining event is gonadarche — gonadal activation by FSH/LH (HPG axis).

Adrenarche (adrenal androgen production) precedes gonadarche and produces pubic hair, axillary hair, acne — but isn't true puberty. Delayed/precocious puberty are defined by gonadarche timing, not adrenarche.

cards.front: An autoimmune small-bowel disease triggered by gluten, with anti-tTG antibodies and villous atrophy, is [___].
cards.context:
An autoimmune enteropathy driven by gluten in HLA-DQ2/DQ8 individuals.

Screen with anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) IgA plus total serum IgA while still eating gluten (use IgG-based serology only if IgA-deficient — common in coeliac).

Duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy confirms it.

cards.front: A child struggles to rise from a low chair, climb stairs and lift objects overhead. These tasks mainly test [___] muscle groups.
cards.context:
Rising and climbing recruit the hip girdle; lifting overhead recruits the shoulder girdle. This is a common distribution of weakness in myopathies.

The pattern narrows the examination but does not name a particular muscle disease; history and further assessment are still needed.

cards.front: A boy's testis remains undescended at 3 months, so he is referred. Orchidopexy should be performed at [___] months.
cards.context: Spontaneous descent after 3 months is unlikely. Referral then allows orchidopexy between 6 and 12 months, before heat-related germ-cell damage becomes established.

cards.front: Labour triggers a surge in [___] that switches the lung epithelium from secreting fluid to absorbing it.
cards.context:
This is the mechanism behind the caesarean risk factor: without labour the switch is never thrown, so fluid clearance starts late.

The lung epithelium stops secreting chloride and starts absorbing sodium, drawing water out of the airspaces.

cards.front: First-line treatment for infantile haemangioma at a high-risk location (nasal tip, periorbital) is oral [___].
cards.context:
Most infantile haemangiomas involute spontaneously and need only observation.

Oral propranolol is first-line — works on multiple haemangioma drivers (vasoconstriction of the active capillary bed, VEGF/bFGF blockade, endothelial apoptosis in the proliferative phase).
